newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wheat promoter sees smut issue being resolved.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wheat promoter sees smut issue being resolved.

text.p: Winston Wilson, outgoing president of U.S. Wheat Associates, said Friday he thought the United States and China would resolve the controversial issue of TCK smut in the next six months.

Addressing the annual conference of the National Association of Wheat Growers, Wilson said he hoped the issue would be resolved as part of China's effort to gain membership to the World Trade Organization.
"We're still hopeful that at some time in the next six months... that we do in fact finally at long last see a solution to the problem with TCK," Wilson said.

TCK smut is a fungal disease found primarily in the Pacific Northwest states of Washington, Oregon and Idaho. China has long banned imports of wheat from the Pacific Northwest because of worries that the fungus is dangerous if consumed by humans.
The U.S. grain industry said it has proven that the disease poses no risk to human health, and many in the U.S. industry believe China uses the issue as a non-tariff trade barrier.

Wilson, who has been president of the non-government marketing organization since 1981, said TCK smut was just one reason that made 1996 a challenging and sometimes difficult year for his organization.

"Now that the World Trade Organization is coming together, we've got a lot of work to do," Wilson said. "Many countries are replacing former trade barriers with numerous phytosanitary concerns which are in most cases not really phytosanitary concerns but a good way to keep imports down."
Wilson criticized the way foreign wheat marketing boards ate into U.S. wheat export markets.
He specifically referred to the Australian Wheat Board's recent move to sell wheat to India at around 60 cents below the market value.
He also explained reasons for the lackluster U.S. wheat export lineup for the second half of the marketing year.

"There are several reasons for this. Buyers are not certain which way the price is going to go," Wilson said. "There's also been a lot of discussion about instituting the (Export Enhancement Program), and some of our buyers who were former recipients of EEP are very possibly waiting to see how that comes out before they commit."

Wilson said the continued trend of nations privatizing their wheat-buying operations presented new opportunities but also hurdles for U.S. wheat exports. He noted that global customers were becoming more specific about wanting different milling qualities of wheat.
"We have a new and very different customer.. and the fact of the matter is that he's going to buy what he thinks he needs wherever he has to go to get it," Wilson said.

"We've got to take a serious look at how we treat wheat varieties and how we pick the ones we want to plant," Wilson said. "I would not be surprised if within five years we're... seeing export customers contracting for specific varieties. We need to get ready for that."
He also said the new U.S. farm legislation, which lifted most federal controls on crop acreage in exchange for a cap on annual subsidy spending, would lead to increasingly volatile grain markets.

"(The new legislation) is going to provide us with a lot of instability with both prices and supplies," Wilson said. "We're not going to have the normal guaranteed wheat acreage, year in and year out."
